title: Pest on foot: the Basilica, the Parliament and the Great Synagogue, and which ticket each one needs
subtitle: Three great buildings within half an hour of each other, and three different ways of being let in.
excerpt: How to visit St Stephen's Basilica, the Hungarian Parliament and the Dohány Street Synagogue in one walk through Pest: what each ticket covers, which visit must be booked for a fixed time, and what is free between them.
secondary_keywords: Hungarian Parliament tour how to book

meta_title: Pest on foot: Basilica, Parliament, Synagogue tickets
meta_description: St Stephen's Basilica, the Parliament and the Dohány Street Synagogue in one walk: what each ticket covers and which visit needs a fixed time.

featured_image.alt: The front of St Stephen's Basilica in Budapest, with its two bell towers and its dome, seen across the square

content_html:
[place attraction="st-stephen-s-basilica" city="budapest"]

On a January day in 1868 the dome of the great church that Pest had been building for seventeen years fell in. The first architect, József Hild, had died the year before. His successor, Miklós Ybl, had found cracks in the walls and stopped the work, and nobody was hurt. Ybl pulled down much of what stood and started again to a new design. He too died before the end, and St Stephen's Basilica was finished only in 1905, more than half a century after it was begun.

Its dome is 96 metres high. So is the dome of the Parliament, a quarter of an hour away on the river. The number is deliberate: it recalls 896, the year from which Hungarians date their arrival in the country, and no building in the centre was to rise higher. Add the Great Synagogue in Dohány Street and you have the three great buildings of Pest, all within a half-hour walk. Each lets visitors in by a different system, and only one of them can be left to chance.

The Basilica: three things behind one name

The square in front is free, and so is the outside. To go in as a visitor you need a ticket, and there are three kinds:

  • the church, meaning the main hall under the dome;
  • the panoramic terrace and the treasury, which are reached separately, by lift for most of the way or by a long staircase;
  • a combined ticket for all of it.

The ticket office is not at the church door. It is in a building on the square, and vouchers bought elsewhere are exchanged there too, so look for it first.

Inside, the thing people come for is in a chapel to the left of the high altar: the Holy Right, the mummified right hand of King Stephen, who founded the Hungarian state and died in 1038. The terrace runs around the outside of the dome.

The church is used for worship. On Sunday mornings it is given over to mass and visits begin after midday, and on Saturdays weddings can close the main hall for a while.

The dome of the basilica from below. The first one fell in while it was being built. Photo: Jules Verne Times Two, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The Parliament: only with a tour, at a fixed time

The Parliament was built between 1885 and 1904 to the designs of Imre Steindl. It is 268 metres long and has 691 rooms, and you cannot walk into it. Visitors go round on a tour of about 45 minutes, in a group, at the time printed on the ticket, with a guide or an audio guide in the language chosen when booking.

The tour starts from the visitor centre, which is underground at the northern end of the building. It takes in the main staircase, the hall under the dome, where the Holy Crown of Hungary is kept under guard, and the chamber of the former upper house.

  • Tickets are for a slot and a language, and in season the good ones are gone days ahead. This is the visit to book first, and to plan the rest of the day around.
  • Citizens of the European Economic Area are charged a lower rate than other visitors and have to show a document.
  • There is a security check, as at an airport.
  • Tours are cancelled or cut short when the building is needed for sittings or state events.

Our partner does not sell the Parliament tour. Its audio walks describe the building from outside.

The Parliament from Kossuth Square. The square is free; the inside is seen only on a timed tour. Photo: A.Donaire2005, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.

The Great Synagogue in Dohány Street

The synagogue was built between 1854 and 1859 to the designs of the Viennese architect Ludwig Förster, in a Moorish style, with two onion-domed towers. It seats about three thousand people and is the largest synagogue in Europe.

One ticket covers the whole enclosure: the synagogue, the Hungarian Jewish Museum beside it, the Heroes' Temple, the garden, and the memorial park behind. The garden is a cemetery, which is unusual beside a synagogue. In the winter of 1944 to 1945 this was the edge of the Budapest ghetto, and more than two thousand of the people who died there were buried in the courtyard. In the park stands a weeping willow of metal by the sculptor Imre Varga, with the names of victims on its leaves.

The synagogue is closed to visitors on Saturdays and on Jewish holidays, and it closes early on Fridays. Men are asked to cover their heads (a paper kippah is handed out), shoulders and knees should be covered, and bags are checked at the gate.

Inside the Dohány Street Synagogue, with its two tiers of galleries. Photo: Suicasmo, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

What is free along the way

Kossuth Square, around the Parliament, is open to everyone. A few minutes south along the embankment are the Shoes on the Danube Bank: sixty pairs of iron shoes at the water's edge, placed in 2005 in memory of the people shot into the river by Arrow Cross militiamen in 1944 and 1945. From there Liberty Square and the streets of the fifth district lead to the Basilica in ten minutes.

The Shoes on the Danube Bank, a few minutes south of the Parliament. Photo: Marek Mróz, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The walk, in order

Take the Parliament slot first, in the morning. Walk south to the Shoes, cut inland through Liberty Square to the Basilica, then go on past Deák Ferenc Square to Dohány Street. The whole line is about two and a half kilometres. With the three visits it fills a long half day. On a Saturday, leave out the synagogue or see it another day. On a Sunday, put the Basilica in the afternoon.

Reading the partner's listings

  • The Basilica ticket with a city walk audio tour lets you choose between the church ticket and the one for church, dome and treasury. The audio is a walk through the city afterwards. It does not cover the inside of the church.
  • The Basilica entry with an organ concert adds a meeting with the organist and a short concert, at a set time. The voucher is exchanged at the ticket office on the square, so come early.
  • The Dohány Synagogue ticket with a sightseeing audio tour is the entrance ticket plus an audio walk through the city. Again, there is no commentary inside.
  • The audio walks (Jewish heritage, the landmarks of Pest, the Pest heritage trail) are commentary only, in the partner's app. They pass all three buildings and enter none. Bring earphones.

These are the tickets and audio walks our partner sells for this part of Budapest, with today's prices:

[partner city="budapest" match="basilica,organ,stephen,synagogue,landmarks,heritage,jewish" limit="6"]

Hours change with the season and with services: the current ones are on our page for St Stephen's Basilica.

From here

Andrássy Avenue starts behind the Basilica and runs straight to Heroes' Square, past the Opera and the House of Terror. At its far end, in the City Park, is the Széchenyi Thermal Bath. See what else there is in Budapest, or open the trip planner for Hungary.

Cover photo: P. Hughes, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.

faqs.q: Is St Stephen's Basilica in Budapest free to enter?
faqs.a: The square and the outside are free. To go in as a visitor you need a ticket: one for the church, one for the panoramic terrace and treasury, or a combined one. The ticket office is in a building on the square.

faqs.q: How do you visit the Hungarian Parliament?
faqs.a: Only on a tour of about 45 minutes, in a group, at the time on your ticket, starting from the visitor centre at the northern end of the building. Book the slot ahead, because in season they sell out days in advance.

faqs.q: What does the Dohány Street Synagogue ticket include?
faqs.a: The synagogue, the Hungarian Jewish Museum, the Heroes' Temple, the garden cemetery and the memorial park with the metal weeping willow.

faqs.q: Is the Dohány Street Synagogue open on Saturdays?
faqs.a: No. It is closed to visitors on Saturdays and on Jewish holidays, and it closes early on Fridays.

faqs.q: Can you see the Basilica, the Parliament and the Synagogue in one day?
faqs.a: Yes. They lie on a line of about two and a half kilometres. Book the Parliament tour for the morning, then walk to the Basilica and on to the synagogue, which together fill a long half day.

title: Fisherman's Bastion and Castle Hill in Budapest: what is free, what needs a ticket, and how to get up
subtitle: A fortress that never defended anything, a church with a tiled roof, a palace full of museums, and a hill you can climb four ways.
excerpt: What you can see for nothing on Castle Hill in Budapest and what needs a ticket: Fisherman's Bastion, Matthias Church and the Royal Palace, with the ways up the hill and a route from the Vienna Gate to the palace terrace.
secondary_keywords: Buda Castle Hill what is free
how to get to Buda Castle
longtail_phrases: is Fisherman's Bastion free to visit
do you need a ticket for Buda Castle
how to get up to Castle Hill in Budapest
is Matthias Church worth the ticket
when is the best time to visit Fisherman's Bastion
meta_title: Fisherman's Bastion and Castle Hill: free or ticket
meta_description: What is free on Castle Hill in Budapest and what needs a ticket: Fisherman's Bastion, Matthias Church, the Royal Palace, and four ways up the hill.

featured_image.alt: The white conical turrets and arcades of Fisherman's Bastion in Budapest above green trees, under a blue sky

content_html:
[place attraction="matthias-church" city="budapest"]

Fisherman's Bastion looks like the oldest thing on Castle Hill, and it is one of the newest. It was built between 1895 and 1902 by the architect Frigyes Schulek, who had just finished restoring the church beside it, as a terrace from which to look at the city. Its seven turrets stand for the seven Magyar chieftains who led their people into the country a thousand years earlier.

The name is older than the stones. In the Middle Ages this stretch of the town wall is said to have been defended by the guild of fishermen, who lived below it by the river. Schulek's bastion never defended anything. It was made for a view, and that leads to the question most visitors ask on the way up: how much of this hill do you have to pay for?

Fisherman's Bastion: free below, a ticket above

Most of it is free at all hours: the stairs that climb from the river side, the lower terraces, the arcades and the square behind, with the bronze statue of King Stephen on horseback.

A small ticket is asked only for the upper walkway and its turrets, and only during the day. Early in the morning and in the evening the barrier is open and nobody charges. The hours of the paid window change with the season.

The view from the free terraces is nearly the same as from the top level, which is a few metres higher. Part of the terrace is taken up by a café, where the price of the view is a drink.

What people climb for: the river and the Parliament from the bastion. Photo: Dguendel, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.

Matthias Church: a ticket, and a second one for the tower

Its official name is the Church of Our Lady. It is called after King Matthias Corvinus, who was married here in the fifteenth century and added to the building. When the Ottomans took Buda in 1541 it became the city's main mosque, and it stayed one for nearly a century and a half. In 1867 Franz Joseph and Elisabeth were crowned king and queen of Hungary in it, to a mass that Franz Liszt wrote for the day. The last Habsburg ruler, Charles IV, was crowned here in 1916.

What you see today is largely Schulek's work of the 1870s to 1890s: he rebuilt the church in a Gothic style and covered the roof with glazed tiles from the Zsolnay factory in Pécs. Inside, every wall and pillar is painted with patterns.

  • The church needs a ticket. It is sold at an office across the square, not at the door.
  • The bell tower is a separate ticket: a guided climb at set times, up nearly two hundred steps.
  • Visits stop for services. On Sunday mornings and on days with weddings or concerts the hours are shorter.

The glazed tiles of the roof of Matthias Church. Photo: kallerna, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The Royal Palace: free outside, museums inside

The southern end of the hill is the Royal Palace. It was shelled to ruins in the siege of Budapest in the winter of 1944 to 1945, and rebuilt afterwards in a plainer form with a new dome. It is not furnished as a palace. Its wings hold the Hungarian National Gallery, the Budapest History Museum and the national library, each with its own ticket.

The courtyards and terraces are free: the long terrace above the river, the statue of the mythical Turul bird, and the Matthias Fountain, which shows the king out hunting. For some years the whole district has been a building site, as parts destroyed in the war are put up again. Expect cranes and fences, and check which rooms and museums are open before you count on one.

The Royal Palace from the Pest side of the river. Photo: Paul Colin Hennig, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Four ways up the hill

  • The funicular. It has run since 1870 from Clark Ádám Square, at the Buda end of the Chain Bridge, to the gate of the palace. The ride lasts a minute or two, it needs its own ticket, and in season the queue is longer than the walk.
  • The bus. Line 16 climbs from Deák Ferenc Square in Pest, over the Chain Bridge, to Dísz Square in the middle of the hill, on an ordinary public transport ticket.
  • On foot. Paths and stairs lead up from Clark Ádám Square in ten to fifteen minutes. From the north, the streets rise gently from Széll Kálmán Square, on metro line M2, to the Vienna Gate.
  • Escalators. At the Castle Garden Bazaar, on the river below the palace, escalators and a lift go up through the gardens.

Cars need a permit to enter the district, so do not plan on a taxi to the church door.

A carriage of the funicular, which first ran in 1870. Photo: Jakub Hałun, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

A route from north to south

The hill is a narrow plateau about a kilometre and a half long, with the old town at the northern end and the palace at the southern. Walked from the top end, the route runs downhill.

Start at the Vienna Gate. Follow the quiet streets of Baroque houses, Táncsics Mihály Street or Fortuna Street, to Holy Trinity Square, where the church and the bastion stand. Go on along Tárnok Street to Dísz Square, pass Sándor Palace, the office of the president, and come out on the terrace of the Royal Palace. Leave by the funicular, the paths or the Garden Bazaar. Without going inside anything it takes about two hours.

What our partner sells here

All of these are audio walks in the partner's app, on your own phone. None includes a ticket to the church, the turrets or a museum, so everything above still applies.

  • The Castle Hill walk starts at the Vienna Gate and stays on the hill.
  • The other walks begin in Pest, at the Basilica, at the Parliament or on Andrássy Avenue, and reach the hill at the end. They are longer city walks, of two to three and a half hours.

Choose by where the walk starts and how long it is, and bring earphones. These are the audio walks our partner sells for Castle Hill, with today's prices:

[partner attraction="matthias-church" match="castle,heights,hill,twin,boulevards" limit="5"]

When to go

The hill faces east over the river. In the morning you look into the sun, and the Parliament is a silhouette. From mid-afternoon the light falls on Pest, and after dark the bridges and the Parliament are lit. Tour groups fill the bastion from mid-morning to late afternoon. At sunrise it is empty, and the upper level is free. Current hours are on our page for Matthias Church.

From here

Go down to the Chain Bridge, the first permanent bridge between Buda and Pest, opened in 1849, and cross it on foot: the Basilica is ten minutes beyond. For the museums of the palace, see our page for Buda Castle. See what else there is in Budapest, or open the attractions map of Hungary.

Cover photo: Perituss, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

faqs.q: Is Fisherman's Bastion free?
faqs.a: Most of it is: the stairs, the lower terraces and the arcades are free at all hours. Only the upper walkway and turrets need a small ticket, and only during the day. Early in the morning and in the evening they are open without charge.

faqs.q: Do you need a ticket for Buda Castle?
faqs.a: Not for the hill, the streets, the courtyards or the terraces of the Royal Palace. Tickets are needed for the museums inside the palace, for Matthias Church and for its tower.

faqs.q: How do you get up to Castle Hill in Budapest?
faqs.a: By the funicular from Clark Ádám Square, by bus 16 from Deák Ferenc Square, on foot in ten to fifteen minutes from the Chain Bridge, or by the escalators of the Castle Garden Bazaar. The funicular has its own ticket and often a queue.

faqs.q: Is Fisherman's Bastion old?
faqs.a: No. It was built between 1895 and 1902 by Frigyes Schulek as a viewing terrace. Its seven turrets stand for the seven Magyar chieftains.

faqs.q: When is the best time to visit Fisherman's Bastion?
faqs.a: At sunrise it is empty and the upper level is free. For photographs of the Parliament, come from mid-afternoon, when the light falls on Pest, or after dark.

title: Kazimierz and Podgórze in Kraków on foot: a route, what is free, and what needs a ticket
subtitle: The old Jewish town, the footbridge, the square of empty chairs. One walk in two halves, with the river between them.
excerpt: A walking route through Kazimierz and across the Vistula to Podgórze in Kraków: the synagogues and what each asks at the door, the memorials that are free, why the Schindler Factory has to be booked, and what the partner sells here.
secondary_keywords: Kazimierz Jewish quarter what to see
longtail_phrases: what to see in Kazimierz Krakow on foot
are the synagogues in Kazimierz free
how far is Schindler Factory from Kazimierz
where was the Krakow ghetto
is Kazimierz open on Saturday
meta_title: Kazimierz and Podgórze in Kraków: a walk, free or ticket
meta_description: A route through Kazimierz and over the river to Podgórze: the synagogues, the free memorials, the Schindler Factory, and what needs a ticket.

featured_image.alt: The red brick Old Synagogue in Kazimierz, Kraków, with its crenellated parapet and green copper porch roof

content_html:
[place attraction="old-synagogue-krakow" city="krakow"]

In 1335 King Casimir the Great founded a new town on an island in the Vistula, just south of the royal castle of Kraków, and gave it his own name. Kazimierz had its own walls, its own town hall and its own market square. In 1495 the Jews of Kraków were ordered to move there, into the eastern part of the town, and for four and a half centuries a Jewish quarter and a Christian one stood side by side, a few streets apart.

By 1939 about a quarter of the people of Kraków were Jewish. In March 1941 the German occupiers forced those who were still in the city across the river, into a ghetto of a few streets in the district of Podgórze. By March 1943 the ghetto had been emptied. Kazimierz was left standing and hollow, and stayed that way for decades, until Steven Spielberg filmed Schindler's List in its streets in 1993 and visitors began to come. The walk that tells this story has two halves, with the river between them. Most of it is free.

Szeroka Street: the heart of Jewish Kazimierz

Szeroka means wide, and the street is more a long square than a street. At its southern end stands the Old Synagogue, a fortified brick building begun in the fifteenth century, the oldest synagogue still standing in Poland. It is no longer a place of worship: it is a branch of the city's museum, on the history and customs of the Jews of Kraków, with a ticket.

Halfway up the square is the small Remuh Synagogue, founded in the 1550s and still in use. A modest fee is asked at the gate, which also opens the cemetery behind. Rabbi Moses Isserles, known as the Remuh, is buried there, and pilgrims leave notes on his grave. One wall of the cemetery is built from fragments of tombstones broken during the war.

The old cemetery behind the Remuh Synagogue. Photo: Kritzolina, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The other synagogues

Kazimierz has seven synagogues within a few minutes of each other, among them the Isaac, the High, the Kupa and the Tempel, on Miodowa Street, with its gilded interior of the 1860s. Each has its own door, its own small fee and its own hours, and no single ticket covers them all. Those in religious use are closed on Saturdays and on Jewish holidays. Men are asked to cover their heads.

Plac Nowy and the Christian side

Five minutes west is Plac Nowy, the market square of the quarter. The round brick hall in the middle was built in 1900, and between the wars it served as a kosher poultry slaughterhouse. Today its hatches sell zapiekanki, long toasted open sandwiches, and the square around it is ringed with bars.

Go on south to Plac Wolnica, the old market square of Christian Kazimierz. The former town hall on it houses the Ethnographic Museum, on the folk life of Poland, and a second building of the museum, Esterka's House on Krakowska Street, shows temporary exhibitions. Both have tickets. The huge Gothic church of Corpus Christi, a street away, is free to enter.

The round hall of Plac Nowy, built in 1900. Photo: Mach240390, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.

Over the river to Podgórze

From the end of Mostowa Street the Father Bernatek footbridge, opened in 2010, crosses the Vistula. Sculpted acrobats balance on its cables. On the far bank, to the left, a block of rusted steel hangs over an old power station: Cricoteka, the centre devoted to the theatre director and artist Tadeusz Kantor. It is a museum of twentieth-century art, with a ticket, and has nothing to do with the war.

The footbridge from Kazimierz to Podgórze. Photo: Jakub Hałun, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Ten minutes east is Ghetto Heroes Square. This was the main square of the ghetto, where people were gathered before the transports. Since 2005 it has been set with large empty metal chairs. On its corner is the Eagle Pharmacy, whose owner, Tadeusz Pankiewicz, kept it open inside the ghetto and used it to help the people shut in there. It is now a small museum, with a ticket.

A fragment of the ghetto wall stands on Lwowska Street, five minutes south. Its top is cut in arches, in the shape of Jewish gravestones.

The empty chairs of Ghetto Heroes Square, in Podgórze. Photo: Ingo Mehling, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The Schindler Factory: book it, or leave it

The enamel factory of Oskar Schindler is on Lipowa Street, ten minutes beyond the square, on the other side of the railway. The museum in its office building is about Kraków under occupation from 1939 to 1945 as a whole. Schindler and the people he saved are one part of it.

It is the one place on this walk that cannot be left to chance. Entry is by ticket for a fixed time, numbers are limited, and in season the slots are sold out days ahead. Reserve before you plan the day, and allow an hour and a half inside. Without a slot, the walk still makes sense: the factory building, the square and the wall are all seen from the street.

What our partner sells here

  • Three audio walks, in the partner's app on your own phone: one through Kazimierz and its synagogues, one from Kazimierz to the ghetto and the Schindler Factory, and one on Kraków in the Second World War. They are commentary only. The one that has the factory in its title does not include entry to it, and none includes a synagogue.
  • Three entry tickets: the Ethnographic Museum on Plac Wolnica, its second building at Esterka's House, and Cricoteka.

Bring earphones for the walks. These are the audio walks and tickets our partner sells for this part of Kraków, with today's prices:

[partner city="krakow" match="kazimierz,echoes,schindler,ghetto,jewish,ethnographic,esterka,cricoteka" limit="6"]

How long, and which day

  • Szeroka Street is twenty minutes on foot from the Main Market Square, or a few stops by tram.
  • From Szeroka to the footbridge is ten minutes, from the bridge to Ghetto Heroes Square ten more, and the factory another ten. The whole line is under three kilometres.
  • With one synagogue and the factory, allow half a day.
  • Avoid Saturday if the synagogues matter to you. Several of the city's museums close or change their rules on Mondays, so check that day too.

Current hours are on our page for the Old Synagogue.

From here

Wawel Castle is ten minutes north of Kazimierz, at the end of Stradom Street, and the Old Town begins behind it. In the evening Kazimierz itself is where much of the city goes to eat. See what else there is in Kraków, or open the trip planner for Poland.

Cover photo: Marcin Konsek, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

faqs.q: What is there to see in Kazimierz in Kraków?
faqs.a: Szeroka Street with the Old Synagogue and the Remuh Synagogue and cemetery, five more synagogues, the round market hall of Plac Nowy, and Plac Wolnica with the Ethnographic Museum. Across the footbridge are Ghetto Heroes Square and the Schindler Factory.

faqs.q: Are the synagogues in Kazimierz free?
faqs.a: Mostly not. Each has its own door, its own small fee and its own hours, and no single ticket covers them all. The Old Synagogue is a museum with a ticket.

faqs.q: How far is the Schindler Factory from Kazimierz?
faqs.a: About half an hour on foot from Szeroka Street: ten minutes to the footbridge, ten to Ghetto Heroes Square and ten more to Lipowa Street.

faqs.q: Where was the Kraków ghetto?
faqs.a: Not in Kazimierz but across the river, in Podgórze. It existed from March 1941 to March 1943. Ghetto Heroes Square, the Eagle Pharmacy and a fragment of the wall on Lwowska Street mark it today.

faqs.q: Do you need to book the Schindler Factory in advance?
faqs.a: Yes. Entry is by ticket for a fixed time, numbers are limited, and in season the slots sell out days ahead.

title: From Old Town Square to Charles Bridge on foot: what is free in Prague's centre, and which tower to climb
subtitle: One kilometre of the old coronation route, a clock that performs every hour, and two towers that both sell a view.
excerpt: A walk along the Royal Route in Prague from the Powder Tower to Charles Bridge: what costs nothing, what the Old Town Hall ticket covers, how the two towers compare, and what the partner sells along the way.
focus_keyword: Old Town Square to Charles Bridge walk
secondary_keywords: Prague Old Town Hall tower or bridge tower
what is free in Prague Old Town
longtail_phrases: how long is the walk from Old Town Square to Charles Bridge
is the Prague astronomical clock free
which tower to climb in Prague Old Town
is Charles Bridge free

meta_title: Old Town Square to Charles Bridge: which tower to climb
meta_description: A walk on Prague's Royal Route from the Powder Tower to Charles Bridge: what is free, what the Old Town Hall ticket covers, and which tower to climb.

featured_image.alt: Charles Bridge and the Old Town Bridge Tower in Prague seen from the river in warm low light, with a green church dome behind

content_html:
[place attraction="charles-bridge" city="prague"]

The first stone of the bridge was laid by the emperor Charles IV himself, in 1357, on the ninth day of July, at 5.31 in the morning. The moment is said to have been chosen by his astrologers. Written out as year, day, month, hour and minute it gives 1 3 5 7 9 7 5 3 1, a row of odd numbers that climbs and comes down again.

The bridge replaced an older one that a flood had carried away in 1342, and until 1841 it was the only way across the Vltava in Prague. Every king of Bohemia crossed it on the day of his coronation, at the end of a procession that began at the eastern gate of the Old Town and wound through its streets. That line, the Royal Route, is still the walk everybody takes. It is short and it costs nothing. What takes thought is the things along it that sell tickets, above all the two towers.

The route in one paragraph

Begin at the Powder Tower, the dark Gothic gate at the edge of the Old Town. Walk down Celetná Street to Old Town Square, leave the square by the corner under the clock, cross the Little Square, and follow Karlova Street as it twists to the river. It ends at a small square in front of the Old Town Bridge Tower, and the bridge begins under the tower's arch. To this point it is about a kilometre. The bridge adds half a kilometre more. Without stops it is a walk of twenty minutes, and with them it takes half a morning.

Old Town Square: the clock is free, the tower is not

The astronomical clock on the wall of the Old Town Hall was first set up in 1410. Its upper dial shows the position of the sun and the moon, and the lower one is a calendar. On every hour from nine in the morning to eleven at night two small windows open and the twelve apostles file past. The show lasts well under a minute and is free. The crowd in front of it is the densest in the city, and pickpockets work there.

The astronomical dial of the clock, first set up in 1410. Photo: Godot13, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The ticket for the Old Town Hall covers more than a view. It includes the tower, which has a lift, the historic halls, the chapel, from which you see the apostles from behind, and the cellars under the building. The gallery of the tower looks straight down on the square.

Across the square, the church of Our Lady before Týn asks for no ticket, only a donation. It keeps limited hours and is closed on Mondays. The way in is not obvious: a passage under the arcaded houses in front of it. The astronomer Tycho Brahe, who died in Prague in 1601, is buried inside. The memorial to Jan Hus in the middle of the square was unveiled in 1915, five hundred years after his death at the stake.

Old Town Square after dark: the tower of the Old Town Hall on the left, the Týn church at the end. Photo: Diliff, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

The spires of the Týn church. The way in is through a passage under the houses in front of it. Photo: Scotch Mist, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Karlova Street and the Klementinum

Karlova is narrow, crooked and lined with souvenir shops from end to end. Walk it for its shape, not for its windows. Along its northern side runs the wall of the Klementinum, the former Jesuit college, one of the largest groups of buildings in the city. Its Baroque library hall and its astronomical tower are shown only on guided tours, with a ticket, at set times.

Charles Bridge and its towers

The bridge is free and open at all hours. It is 516 metres long and stands on sixteen arches. The thirty statues along its parapets were added mostly between 1683 and 1714, and most of those you see are copies. The oldest is the bronze of St John of Nepomuk, a priest who was thrown from the bridge into the river in 1393 on the orders of King Wenceslas IV. People touch the plaque beneath it for luck, and a small cross on the parapet nearby marks the place where he went over.

There is a tower at each end, and both can be climbed with a ticket. The Old Town Bridge Tower, on the side you arrive from, has 138 steps and no lift. Its gallery looks along the whole length of the bridge to the castle. The towers at the Lesser Town end give the same view in reverse.

The bridge at sunrise, the one hour when it is empty. Photo: mendhak, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.

Which tower to climb

  • The Old Town Hall tower has a lift, a wide gallery and the square at its foot. It is the busier of the two, and its ticket also opens the rooms of the town hall.
  • The Old Town Bridge Tower is a climb on foot. Its view is the classic one of Prague: the river, the bridge with its statues, and the castle on the hill behind.

If stairs are a difficulty, take the town hall. If you want one photograph of the city, take the bridge tower.

Reading the partner's listings

  • Charles Bridge with a mobile guide and tower admission is entry to the Old Town Bridge Tower with a guide on your phone. A virtual reality show is an optional extra. The listing gives few details, and the address it names is in the Old Town, not at the bridge, so read where the ticket is collected.
  • The Astronomical Clock ticket with a city audio tour is entry to the Old Town Hall at a set time, with a short introduction on the spot and not a guided tour. The audio walk that comes with it goes on through the city, over the bridge and up towards the castle. It does not cover the inside.
  • The Old Town and Jewish Quarter audio tours are commentary only. Tickets to the synagogues of the Jewish Museum are not part of them.
  • The other audio walks follow longer loops through the centre. Bring earphones.

These are the tickets and audio walks our partner sells along this route, with today's prices:

[partner city="prague" match="josefov,jewish,quarter,astronomical,clock,charles,bridge,heart" limit="6"]

When to walk it

Before eight in the morning the bridge is nearly empty and the light comes from behind you onto the castle. From ten until dusk it is a slow river of people, with painters and musicians along the sides. If you want to watch the clock, stand well back on the square a few minutes before the hour: the figures are small and close up you see less. Current hours for the towers are on our pages for the astronomical clock and Charles Bridge.

From here

At the far end of the bridge the Royal Route goes on through the Lesser Town and climbs to Prague Castle, half an hour uphill. To the right of the bridge, on the Old Town side, the former Jewish quarter is ten minutes away. See what else there is in Prague, or open the trip planner for Czechia.

Cover photo: Ввласенко, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

faqs.q: How long is the walk from Old Town Square to Charles Bridge?
faqs.a: About ten minutes along Karlova Street, a little over half a kilometre. The whole Royal Route from the Powder Tower to the bridge is about a kilometre.

faqs.q: Is the Prague astronomical clock free?
faqs.a: Watching it from the square is free: the apostles appear on every hour from nine in the morning to eleven at night. A ticket is needed for the Old Town Hall, with its tower, halls, chapel and cellars.

faqs.q: Is Charles Bridge free?
faqs.a: Yes. The bridge is open at all hours without a ticket. Only the towers at its two ends charge for the climb.

faqs.q: Which tower should you climb in the Old Town of Prague?
faqs.a: The Old Town Hall tower has a lift and looks down on the square. The Old Town Bridge Tower has 138 steps and no lift, and looks along the bridge to the castle. Choose the first if stairs are a problem, the second for the classic view.

faqs.q: When is Charles Bridge empty?
faqs.a: Early in the morning, before about eight. From mid-morning until dusk it is crowded all year.

title: Tallinn's old town on foot: the Lower Town, Toompea, and what is free on the way
subtitle: Two medieval towns, one on top of the other, joined by a long leg and a short one.
excerpt: How to walk the old town of Tallinn in half a day: the merchant town below, the hill of Toompea above, the two lanes that join them, the viewpoints that cost nothing and the towers and churches that sell tickets.

meta_description: A half-day walk through the old town of Tallinn: the Lower Town, the two lanes up to Toompea, the free viewpoints, and the towers that sell tickets.

featured_image.alt: Red-roofed wall towers and church spires of the old town of Tallinn rising out of morning mist

content_html:
[place attraction="tallinn-old-town" city="tallinn"]

For most of its history Tallinn was two towns. On the limestone hill of Toompea, where the Danes built a castle after they took the place in 1219, lived the nobles, the bishop and the officers of whoever ruled the country. At its foot lived the merchants. Their town joined the Hanseatic League in 1285, governed itself by the law of Lübeck, and answered to its own council.

The two did not like each other. A wall ran between them, and the gate in it was locked every night. They were joined into one city only in the 1870s. The arrangement still decides how a visit works: the merchants' town is where the museums and towers that sell tickets are, and the hill is where the views are, free of charge. The whole of it is about a kilometre across.

The Lower Town

Most people come in through the Viru Gate, two round towers at the eastern edge, and walk up Viru Street to Town Hall Square. The town hall on it was finished in 1404 and is the only Gothic town hall left standing in northern Europe. On top of its spire turns Old Thomas, a weathervane in the shape of a soldier, first put up in 1530. The building and its tower are open to visitors mainly in summer, with a ticket.

On the corner of the square is the Town Hall Pharmacy, which has been in business on the same spot since at least 1422. It still sells medicines, and a back room of old jars and instruments is free to look at.

Merchant houses on Town Hall Square, in the Lower Town. Photo: Cayambe, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

North of the square runs Pikk Street, the street of the guilds, with the Great Guild Hall, now a history museum, and the church of the Holy Spirit, which has a painted clock of the 1680s on its outside wall. At the far end are St Olaf's Church and the squat gun tower called Fat Margaret, which holds the maritime museum. In the sixteenth century the spire of St Olaf was among the tallest in Europe. Its tower can be climbed in the warm months, by a narrow stair of more than two hundred and fifty steps, with a ticket. The church itself is free.

The wall and its towers

Tallinn has kept most of its medieval defences: nearly two kilometres of wall and about twenty towers. You see them best for nothing, from the park along the outside of the north-western stretch. A short section of the wall-walk, between three of the towers there, is open with a ticket, and there is another on the eastern side, above the lane where knitted goods are sold.

Towers of the town wall, from above. Photo: Ad Meskens, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Two ways up: the Long Leg and the Short Leg

Two lanes join the towns. Pikk jalg, the Long Leg, is a sloping street between high walls, made for carts and riders. It passes under a square gate tower of 1380, the one that was locked at night. Lühike jalg, the Short Leg, is a flight of steps for people on foot, with a gate of its own. Because it has one long leg and one short, the people of Tallinn say that their city limps. Go up by one and come down by the other.

The gate tower of Pikk jalg, the Long Leg, once locked every night. Photo: Ymblanter, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Toompea

At the top of the Long Leg stands the Alexander Nevsky Cathedral, a Russian Orthodox church with onion domes, finished in 1900, when Estonia was a province of the tsar's empire. It is a working church and free to enter.

Opposite is Toompea Castle. Behind its pink Baroque front of the 1770s sits the Riigikogu, the parliament of Estonia, and it is not open to people walking in.

The Dome Church, St Mary's, is the oldest church in the city and the burial place of the nobility of Toompea. Its walls are hung with their carved coats of arms. It asks for a ticket.

The two viewpoints

Both are free and open at all hours. Kohtuotsa looks east over the roofs of the Lower Town to the spire of the town hall and the sea. Patkuli looks north, along the line of wall towers to St Olaf's and the harbour. A long staircase runs down from Patkuli to the foot of the hill, near the railway station.

The Lower Town from Toompea: wall towers and the spire of St Olaf. Photo: Ivar Leidus, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0 EE.

On the southern slope, the Danish King's Garden is the spot where, by legend, a red flag with a white cross fell from the sky during the battle of 1219 and became the flag of Denmark. Next to it is Kiek in de Kök, a cannon tower of the 1470s whose name means "peep into the kitchen". The tower and the tunnels under the bastions are a museum, with a ticket.

Free, and not

  • Free: the streets and squares, the gates, both viewpoints, the wall from outside, the Alexander Nevsky Cathedral, the pharmacy, St Olaf's Church at ground level, the Danish King's Garden.
  • With a ticket: the town hall and its tower, the tower of St Olaf, the walk on the wall, the Dome Church, Kiek in de Kök and the tunnels, Fat Margaret, the Great Guild Hall.

Several of the towers open only from spring to autumn. If one of them is your reason for coming, check its season first.

What our partner sells here

For the old town the partner sells audio walks only, in its app on your own phone. None includes an entry ticket, so the list above still applies. Several are close to each other in content: they cross the Lower Town and climb to Toompea and its viewpoints. They differ in where they start (the Viru Gate, Town Hall Square or the church of the Holy Spirit) and in length, from an hour and a half to two hours. Choose by the starting point nearest to where you are staying, and bring earphones.

These are the audio walks our partner sells for the old town of Tallinn, with today's prices:

[partner city="tallinn" match="toompea,medieval,heights,tales,town" limit="6"]

Practical notes

  • The whole walk, without interiors, takes two to three hours. With two paid visits it fills half a day.
  • The streets are cobbled and the hill is steep. In winter the slopes are icy and it is dark by mid-afternoon.
  • In summer, cruise passengers fill the square and the viewpoints from mid-morning to mid-afternoon. Go up to Toompea early or in the evening.

Hours and seasons are on our pages for Tallinn Old Town and Toompea Castle.

From here

The stairs from Patkuli come out near the railway station, with its market hall and, beyond the tracks, the old factory quarter of Telliskivi, now cafés and studios. In the other direction a tram runs from the edge of the old town to Kadriorg, the park and Baroque palace that Peter the Great built for his wife. See what else there is in Tallinn, or open the attractions map of Estonia.

faqs.q: How long do you need for the old town of Tallinn?
faqs.a: Two to three hours for a walk through the Lower Town and up to Toompea without going inside anything. With two paid visits, half a day.

faqs.q: Are the viewing platforms in Tallinn free?
faqs.a: Yes. Kohtuotsa and Patkuli, the two main viewpoints on Toompea, are free and open at all hours.

faqs.q: What is the difference between Toompea and the Lower Town?
faqs.a: Toompea is the hill where the castle, the cathedral and the nobility were. The Lower Town was the separate merchant town at its foot, with its own council and walls. They were joined into one city only in the 1870s.

faqs.q: Can you climb St Olaf's Church tower in Tallinn?
faqs.a: Yes, in the warm months, with a ticket, by a narrow stair of more than two hundred and fifty steps. The church at ground level is free.

faqs.q: Can you walk on the town wall in Tallinn?
faqs.a: On short sections, with a ticket: one between three towers on the north-western side and one on the eastern side. The rest of the wall is seen from the streets and the park outside it.
